entries.042507333cd1bf7ac02ef693223c6052c2a70123: <div sID="gen8554" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Ezra.3" sID="Ezra.3"/> <div eID="gen8554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8555" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8556" type="x-p"/> In the close of the foregoing chapter we left Israel in their cities, but we may well imagine what a bad posture their affairs were in, the ground untilled, the cities in ruins, all out of order; but here we have an account of the early care they took about the re-establishment of religion among them. Thus did they lay the foundation well, and begin their work at the right end. I. They set up an altar, and offered sacrifices upon it, kept the feasts, and contributed towards the rebuilding of the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.1-Ezra.3.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. They laid the foundation of the temple with a mixture of joy and sorrow, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.8-Ezra.3.13">ver. 8-13</reference>. This was the day of small things, which was not to be despised, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">Zech. iv. 10</reference>.
entries.61475ecabf152621b11a6133d2426cda84c18ac6: <div eID="gen8556" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8555" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Renewal of the Sacrifices. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 536.)</title> <div sID="gen8557" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when the seventh month was come, and the children of Israel <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the cities, the people gathered themselves together as one man to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> written in the law of Moses the man of God. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they set the altar upon his bases; for fear <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon them because of the people of those countries: and they offered burnt offerings thereon unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> burnt offerings morning and evening. <hi type="super">4</hi> They kept also the feast of tabernacles, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> written, and <hi type="italic">offered</hi> the daily burnt offerings by number, according to the custom, as the duty of every day required; <hi type="super">5</hi> And afterward <hi type="italic">offered</hi> the continual burnt offering, both of the new moons, and of all the set feasts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that were consecrated, and of every one that willingly offered a freewill offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> From the first day of the seventh month began they to offer burnt offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . But the foundation of the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was not <hi type="italic">yet</hi> laid. <hi type="super">7</hi> They gave money also unto the masons, and to the carpenters; and meat, and drink, and oil, unto them of Zidon, and to them of Tyre, to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea of Joppa, according to the grant that they had of Cyrus king of Persia. <div eID="gen8557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8558" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general assembly of the returned Israelites at Jerusalem, in the <hi type="italic">seventh month,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.1">v. 1</reference>. We may suppose that they came from Babylon in the spring, and must allow at least four months for the journey, for so long Ezra and his company were in coming, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.9">ch. vii. 9</reference>. The seventh month therefore soon came, in which many of the feasts of the Lord were to be solemnized; and then they gathered themselves together by agreement among themselves, rather than by the command of authority, to Jerusalem. Though they had newly come to their cities, and had their hands full of business there, to provide necessaries for themselves and their families, which might have excused them from attending on God's altar till the hurry was a little over, as many foolishly put off their coming to the communion till they are settled in the world, yet such was their zeal for religion, now that they had newly come from under correction for their irreligion, that they left all their business in the country, to attend God's altar; and (which is strange) in this pious zeal they were all of a mind, they came <hi type="italic">as one man.</hi> Let worldly business be postponed to the business of religion and it will prosper the better. <div eID="gen8558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8559" type="x-p"/> II. The care which their leading men took to have an altar ready for them to attend upon. <div eID="gen8559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8560" type="x-p"/> 1. Joshua and his brethren the priests, Zerubbabel and his brethren the princes, built <hi type="italic">the altar of the God of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.2">v. 2</reference>), in the same place (it is likely) where it had stood, upon the same bases, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.3">v. 3</reference>. Bishop Patrick, observing that before the temple was built there seems to have been a tabernacle pitched for the divine service, as was in David's time, not on Mount Moriah, but Mount Sion (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.23">1 Chron. ix. 23</reference>), supposes that this altar was erected there, to be used while the temple was in building. Let us learn hence, (1.) To <hi type="italic">begin with God.</hi> The more difficult and necessitous our case is the more concerned we are to take him along with us in all our ways. If we expect to be directed by his oracles, let him be honoured by our offerings. (2.) To <hi type="italic">do what we can</hi> in the worship of God when <hi type="italic">we cannot do what we would.</hi> They could not immediately have a temple, but they would not be without an altar. Abraham, wherever he came, <hi type="italic">built an altar;</hi> and wherever we come, though we may perhaps want the benefit of the candlestick of preaching, and the showbread of the eucharist, yet, if we bring not the sacrifices of prayer and praise, we are wanting in our duty, for we have an altar that sanctifies the gift ever ready. <div eID="gen8560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8561" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe the reason here given why they hastened to set up the altar: <hi type="italic">Fear was upon them, because of the people of the land.</hi> They were in the midst of enemies that bore ill will to them and their religion, for whom they were an unequal match. And, (1.) <hi type="italic">Though</hi> they were so, yet they built the altar (so some read it); they would not be frightened from their religion by the opposition they were likely to meet with in it. Never let the fear of man bring us into this snare. (2.) <hi type="italic">Because</hi> they were so, therefore they set up the altar. Apprehension of danger should stir us up to our duty. Have we many enemies? Then it is good to have God our friend and to keep up our correspondence with him. This good use we should make of our fears, we should be driven by them to our knees. Even Saul would think himself undone if the enemy should come upon him before he had made his supplication to God, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.12">1 Sam. xii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen8561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8562" type="x-p"/> III. The sacrifices they offered upon the altar. The altar was reared to be used, and they used it accordingly. Let not those that have an altar starve it. <div eID="gen8562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8563" type="x-p"/> 1. They began <hi type="italic">on the first day of the seventh month,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.6">v. 6</reference>. It does not appear that they had any fire from heaven to begin with, as Moses and Solomon had, but common fire served them, as it did the patriarchs. <div eID="gen8563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8564" type="x-p"/> 2. Having begun, they kept up the <hi type="italic">continual burnt-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">morning and evening,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.3">v. 3</reference>. They had known by sad experience what it was to want the comfort of the daily sacrifice to plead in their daily prayers, and now that it was revived they resolved not to let it fall again. The daily lamb typified the Lamb of God, whose righteousness must be our confidence in all our prayers. <div eID="gen8564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8565" type="x-p"/> 3. They observed all the <hi type="italic">set feasts of the Lord,</hi> and offered the sacrifices appointed for each, and particularly <hi type="italic">the feast of tabernacles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.4-Ezra.3.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Now that they had received such great mercy from God that joyful feast was in a special manner seasonable. And now that they were beginning to settle in their cities it might serve well to remind them of their fathers dwelling in tents in the wilderness. That feast also which had a peculiar reference to gospel times (as appears, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.18">Zech. xiv. 18</reference>) was brought, in a special manner, into reputation, now that those times drew on. Of the services of this feast, which continued seven days and had peculiar sacrifices appointed, it is said that they did <hi type="italic">as the duty of every day required</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Num.29.13-Num.29.38">Num. xxix. 13, 17</reference>, &c.), <hi type="italic">Verbum die in die suo—the word, or matter, of the day in its day</hi> (so it is in the original)—a phrase that has become proverbial with those that have used themselves to scripture-language. If the feast of tabernacles was a figure of a gospel conversation, in respect of continual weanedness from the world and joy in God, we may infer that it concerns us all to do the <hi type="italic">work of the day in its day, according as the duty of the day requires,</hi> that is, (1.) We must improve time, by finding some business to do every day that will turn to a good account. (2.) We must improve opportunity, by accommodating ourselves to that which is the proper business of the present day. Every thing is beautiful in its season. The tenth day of this month was the day of atonement, a solemn day, and very seasonable now: it is very probable that they observed it, yet it is not mentioned, nor indeed in all the Old Testament do I remember the least mention of the observance of that day; as if it were enough that we have the law of it in <reference osisRef="Lev.16.1-Lev.16.34">Lev. xvi.</reference>, and the gospel of it, which was the chief intention of it, in the New Testament. <div eID="gen8565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8566" type="x-p"/> 4. They offered <hi type="italic">every man's free-will offering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.5">v. 5</reference>. The law required much, but they brought more; for, though they had little wealth to support the expense of their sacrifices, they had much zeal, and, we may suppose, spared at their own tables that they might plentifully supply God's altar. Happy are those that bring with them out of the furnace of affliction such a holy heat as this. <div eID="gen8566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8567" type="x-p"/> IV. The preparation they made for the building of the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.7">v. 7</reference>. This they applied themselves immediately to; for, while we do what we can, we must still be aiming to do more and better. Tyre and Sidon must now, as of old, furnish them with workmen, and Lebanon with timber, orders for both which they had from Cyrus. What God calls us to we may depend upon his providence to furnish us for.
entries.190de24ad3fd7f3308e13868d9efec7a8cc8f346: <div eID="gen8567" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Foundation of the Temple Laid. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 535.)</title> <div sID="gen8568" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Now in the second year of their coming unto the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, began Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the remnant of their brethren the priests and the Levites, and all they that were come out of the captivity unto Jerusalem; and appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to set forward the work of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> Then stood Jeshua <hi type="italic">with</hi> his sons and his brethren, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together, to set forward the workmen in the house of God: the sons of Henadad, <hi type="italic">with</hi> their sons and their brethren the Levites. <hi type="super">10</hi> And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , they set the priests in their apparel with trumpets, and the Levites the sons of Asaph with cymbals, to praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , after the ordinance of David king of Israel. <hi type="super">11</hi> And they sang together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; because <hi type="italic">he is</hi> good, for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever toward Israel. And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because the foundation of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was laid. <hi type="super">12</hi> But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, <hi type="italic">who were</hi> ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy: <hi type="super">13</hi> So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off. <div eID="gen8568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8569" type="x-p"/> There was no dispute among the returned Jews whether they should build the temple or no; that was immediately resolved on, and that it should be done with all speed; what comfort could they take in their own land if they had not that token of God's presence with them and the record of his name among them? We have here therefore an account of the beginning of that good work. Observe, <div eID="gen8569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8570" type="x-p"/> I. When it was begun-in the second month of the second year, as soon as ever the season of the year would permit (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.8">v. 8</reference>), and when they had ended the solemnities of the passover. They took little more than half a year for making preparation of the ground and materials; so much were their hearts upon it. Note, When any good work is to be done it will be our wisdom to set about it quickly, and not to lose time, yea, though we foresee difficulty and opposition in it. Thus we engage ourselves to it, and engage God for us. Well begun (we say) is half ended. <div eID="gen8570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8571" type="x-p"/> II. Who began it—Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, and their brethren. Then the work of God is likely to go on well when magistrates, ministers, and people, are hearty for it, and agree in their places to promote it. It was God that gave them one heart for this service, and it boded well. <div eID="gen8571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8572" type="x-p"/> III. Who were employed to further it. They appointed the <hi type="italic">Levites to set forward the work</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.8">v. 8</reference>), and they did it by <hi type="italic">setting forward the workmen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.9">v. 9</reference>), and strengthening their hands with good and comfortable words. Note, Those that do not work themselves may yet do good service by quickening and encouraging those that do work. <div eID="gen8572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8573" type="x-p"/> IV. How God was praised at the laying of the foundation of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.10-Ezra.3.11">v. 10, 11</reference>); the priests with the trumpets appointed by Moses, and the Levites with the cymbals appointed by David, made up a concert of music, not to please the ear, but to assist the singing of that everlasting hymn which will never be out of date, and to which our tongues should never be out of tune, <hi type="italic">God is good, and his mercy endureth for ever,</hi> the burden of <reference osisRef="Ps.136.1-Ps.136.26">Ps. cxxxvi.</reference> Let all the streams of mercy be traced up to the fountain. Whatever our condition is, how many soever our griefs and fears, let it be owned that God is good; and, whatever fails, that his mercy fails not. Let this be sung with application, as here; not only his mercy endures for ever, but it endures for ever towards Israel, Israel when captives in a strange land and strangers in their own land. However it be, yet <hi type="italic">God is good to Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Ps. lxxiii. 1</reference>), good to us. Let the reviving of the church's interests, when they seemed dead, be ascribed to the continuance of God's mercy for ever, for therefore the church continues. <div eID="gen8573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8574" type="x-p"/> V. How the people were affected. A remarkable mixture of various affections there was upon this occasion. Different sentiments there were among the people of God, and each expressed himself according to his sentiments, and yet there was no disagreement among them, their minds were not alienated from each other nor the common concern retarded by it. 1. Those that only knew the misery of having no temple at all praised the Lord with shouts of joy when they saw but the foundation of one laid, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.11">v. 11</reference>. To them even this foundation seemed great, and was as life from the dead; to their hungry souls even this was sweet. They shouted, so that <hi type="italic">the noise was heard afar off.</hi> Note, We ought to be thankful for the beginnings of mercy, though we have not yet come to the perfection of it; and the foundations of a temple, after long desolations, cannot but be fountains of joy to every faithful Israelite. 2. Those that remembered the glory of the first temple which Solomon built, and considered how far this was likely to be inferior to that, perhaps in dimensions, certainly in magnificence and sumptuousness, <hi type="italic">wept with a loud voice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">v. 12</reference>. If we date the captivity with the first, from the fourth of Jehoiakim, it was about fifty-two years since the temple was burnt; if from Jeconiah's captivity, it was but fifty-nine. So that many now alive might remember it standing; and a great mercy it was to the captives that they had the lives of so many of their priests and Levites lengthened out, who could tell them what they themselves remembered of the glory of Jerusalem, to quicken them in their return. These lamented the disproportion between this temple and the former. And, (1.) There was some reason for it; and if they turned their tears into the right channel, and bewailed the sin that was the cause of this melancholy change, they did well. Sin sullies the glory of any church or people, and, when they find themselves diminished and brought low, that must bear the blame. (2.) Yet it was their infirmity to mingle those tears with the common joys and so to cast a damp upon them. They <hi type="italic">despised the day of small things,</hi> and were unthankful for the good they enjoyed, because it was not so much as their ancestors had, though it was much more than they deserved. In the harmony of public joys, let not us be jarring strings. It was an aggravation of the discouragement they hereby gave to the people that they were priests and Levites, who should have known and taught others how to be duly affected under various providences, and not to let the remembrance of former afflictions drown the sense of present mercies. This mixture of sorrow and joy here is a representation of this world. Some are bathing in rivers of joy, while others are drowned in floods of tears. In heaven all are singing, and none sighing; in hell all are weeping and wailing, and none rejoicing; but here on earth we can scarcely <hi type="italic">discern the shouts of joy from the noise of the weeping.</hi> Let us learn to <hi type="italic">rejoice with those that do rejoice</hi> and <hi type="italic">weep with those that weep,</hi> and ourselves to rejoice as though we rejoiced not, and weep as though we wept not.  <chapter eID="Ezra.3"/> <div eID="gen8574" type="x-p"/>

entries.b833dc6a1a0840e80cd94f34c48d80a0ad27c0a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4230"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezra.3.1-Ezra.3.13">Ezr 3:1-13</reference>. The Altar Set Up.</title> <div sID="gen6143" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4230"/><hi type="bold">1. when the seventh month was come--</hi>The departure of the returning exiles from Babylon took place in the spring. For some time after their arrival they were occupied in the necessary work of rearing habitations to themselves amid the ruins of Jerusalem and its neighborhood. This preliminary work being completed, they addressed themselves to rebuild the altar of burnt offering. As the seventh month of the sacred year was at hand--corresponding to the latter end of our September--when the feast of tabernacles (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.34">Le 23:34</reference>) fell to be observed, they resolved to celebrate that religious festival, just as if the temple had been fully restored. <div eID="gen6143" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba3921fb17910842f6e809436aff2d869d685188: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4231"/><div sID="gen6144" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4231"/><hi type="bold">2. Jeshua--</hi>the grandson of Seraiah, the high priest, put to death by Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18-2Kgs.25.21">2Ki 25:18-21</reference>). His father, Josedech, had been carried captive to Babylon, and died there, some time before this.<div eID="gen6144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zerubbabel--</hi>was, according to the order of nature, son of Pedaiah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.3.17-1Chr.3.19">1Ch 3:17-19</reference>); but having been brought up by Salathiel, he was called his son.<div eID="gen6145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon--</hi>This was of urgent and immediate necessity, in order, first, to make atonement for their sins; secondly, to obtain the divine blessing on their preparations for the temple, as well as animate their feelings of piety and patriotism for the prosecution of that national work. <div eID="gen6146" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a2e215ccb4f474dda25f40adcc99326a67349ef: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4232"/><div sID="gen6147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4232"/><hi type="bold">3. they set the altar upon his bases--</hi>They reared it upon its old foundation, so that it occupied as nearly as possible the site on which it had formerly stood.<div eID="gen6147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they offered burnt offerings ... morning and evening--</hi>Deeming it their duty to perform the public rites of religion, they did not wait till the temple should be rebuilt and dedicated; but, at the outset, they resumed the daily service prescribed by the law (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.38">Ex 29:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.6.9">Le 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.6.11">11</reference>), as well as observed the annual seasons of solemn observance. <div eID="gen6148" type="x-p"/>
entries.da3194d81aeb079c792de8ba80a9112791355270: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4233"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezra.3.4-Ezra.3.7">Ezr 3:4-7</reference>. Offerings Renewed.</title> <div sID="gen6149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4233"/><hi type="bold">4-6. They kept also the feast of tabernacles ... From the first day of the seventh month--</hi>They revived at that time the daily oblation, and it was on the fifteenth day of that month the feast of tabernacles was held. <div eID="gen6149" type="x-p"/>
entries.e27adc141783daca1c50d717cc89c59787122f93: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4234"/><div sID="gen6150" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4234"/><hi type="bold">7. They gave ... meat ... drink, and oil, unto them of Zidon--</hi>They opened negotiations with the Tyrians for workmen, as well as for timber, on the same terms and with the same views as Solomon had done (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.11">1Ki 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.15">2Ch 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">16</reference>). <div eID="gen6150" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0d219010d726a9f79a6fd37586ff9198d9b6fbb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4235"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezra.3.8-Ezra.3.13">Ezr 3:8-13</reference>. The Foundation of the Temple Laid.</title> <div sID="gen6151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4235"/><hi type="bold">8. appointed the Levites ... to set forward the work--</hi>that is, to act as overseers of the workmen, and to direct and animate the laborers in the various departments. <div eID="gen6151" type="x-p"/>
entries.c92c6fdd38684dbfe8e3f4a59badf8aaa5530bfe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4236"/><div sID="gen6152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4236"/><hi type="bold">9. Jeshua with his sons--</hi>not the high priest, but a Levite (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.40">Ezr 2:40</reference>). To these, as probably distinguished for their mechanical skill and taste, the duty of acting as overseers was particularly committed. <div eID="gen6152" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9d6a37581cc9aad211163b7f9b620d4a6f57cc0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4237"/><div sID="gen6153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4237"/><hi type="bold">12. But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers ... wept with a loud voice--</hi>Those painful emotions were excited by the sad contrast between the prosperous circumstances in which the foundations of the first temple had been laid and the desolate, reduced state of the country and city when the second was begun; between the inferior size and less costliness of the stones used in the foundations of the second (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.9">1Ki 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.7.10">10</reference>), and the much smaller extent of the foundation itself, including all the appurtenances of the building (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.3">Hag 2:3</reference>); between the comparative smallness of their present means and the immense resources of David and Solomon. Perhaps, however, the chief cause of grief was that the second temple would be destitute of those things which formed the great and distinguishing glory of the first; namely, the ark, the shekinah, the Urim and Thummim, &c. Not that this second temple was not a very grand and beautiful structure. But no matter how great its material splendor was, it was inferior in this respect to that of Solomon. Yet the glory of the second far outshone that of the first temple in another and more important point of view, namely, the receiving within its walls the incarnate Saviour (<reference osisRef="Hag.2.9">Hag 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen6153" type="x-p"/>
entries.172b7d912d294bd4b9e8f4132976cf04e06e97dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4238"/><div sID="gen6154" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4238"/><hi type="bold">13. the people could not discern the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people--</hi>Among Eastern people, expressions of sorrow are always very loud and vehement. It is indicated by wailing, the howl of which is sometimes not easily distinguishable from joyful acclamations. <chapter eID="Ezra.3"/>

entries.11efeac04b96a3ce20e4de0ba30cf6cd2e19da95: <div eID="gen14736" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14737" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14738" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14738" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14737" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14739" type="x-p"/> The altar of burnt-offerings is set up, <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.1-Ezr.3.3">Ezr 3:1-3</reference>. They keep the feast of tabernacles, <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.4-Ezr.3.6">Ezr 3:4-6</reference>. They make provision for rebuilding the temple; and lay its foundation in the second month of the second year, <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.7">Ezr 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.8">Ezr 3:8</reference>. Ceremonies observed in laying the foundation, <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.9-Ezr.3.11">Ezr 3:9-11</reference>. Some weep aloud, and others shout for joy, <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.12-Ezr.3.13">Ezr 3:12-13</reference>. <div eID="gen14739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14740" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14741" type="x-p"/> When the seventh month was come - The month Tisri, which answers to the latter part of our September, and beginning of October. It seems that the Israelites had left Babylon about the spring of the year; that on their arrival at Jerusalem they constructed themselves huts and sheds to lodge in among the ruins, in which they must have spent some months. After this they rebuilt the altar of burnt-offerings, and kept the feast of tabernacles, which happened about this time, and continued to offer sacrifices regularly, as if the temple were standing.
entries.7e0ab52e799c0d0a896786b2f266779ab8cb892a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14742" type="x-p"/> Jeshua the son of Jozadak - He was grandson of Seraiah the high priest, who was put to death by Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">2Kgs 25:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.21">2Kgs 25:21</reference>. This Jeshua or Joshua was the first high priest after the captivity.
entries.8379bfe7fee5428717abcc0986aa7ad4adcb4c9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen14742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14743" type="x-p"/> They set the altar upon his bases - Rebuilt it on the same spot on which it had formerly stood. As it was necessary to keep up the Divine worship during the time they should be employed in re-edifying the temple, they first reared this altar of burnt-offerings; and all this they did, "though fear was upon them," because of the unfriendly disposition of their surrounding neighbors.
entries.509043a81d0a88d213ea605515387aa740d264ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen14743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14744" type="x-p"/> They kept also the feast of tabernacles, as it is written - This began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month; but they had begun the regular offerings from the first day of this month, <reference osisRef="Ezr.3.6">Ezr 3:6</reference>. And these were religiously continued all the time they were building the temple.
entries.d85da595178ddd3164ec0ddc2335eeec2f589068: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen14744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14745" type="x-p"/> They gave money also - They copied the conduct of Solomon while he was building his temple; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.11">1Kgs 5:11</reference>. He employed the Tyrians, gave them meat and drink, etc.; and this permission they now had from Cyrus.
entries.db21c37cf599b7ebbb6a9d96c577e68ab9198bbc: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen14745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14746" type="x-p"/> In the second year - The previous time had been employed in clearing the ground, felling timber, hewing stones, and transporting them to the place, and making other necessary preparations for the commencement of the building.
entries.6ff8c3758bb13722ecde016f0523483d1f20aaad: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14747" type="x-p"/> After the ordinance of David - With psalms which he composed, acting in the manner which he directed.
entries.c61c4d0ffac3ee1cba439d73433bed43a67ccc30: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen14747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14748" type="x-p"/> Wept with a loud voice - They saw that the glory had departed from Israel; in their circumstances it was impossible to build such a house as the first temple was; and had this been even possible, still it would have been greatly inferior, because it wanted the ark of the covenant, the heavenly fire, the mercy-seat, the heavenly manna, Aaron's rod that budded, the Divine shechinah, the spirit of prophecy, and most probably the Urim and Thummim. <div eID="gen14748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14749" type="x-p"/> Many shouted for joy - Finding they were now restored to their own land, and to the worship of their God in his own peculiar city: these, in general, had not seen the original temple; and therefore could not feel affected in that way which the elderly people did. <div eID="gen14749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14750" type="x-p"/> The sight must have been very affecting: a whole people, one part crying aloud with sorrow; the other shouting aloud for joy; and on the same occasion too, in which both sides felt an equal interest! The prophet Haggai comforted them on this occasion by assuring them that the glory of this latter house should exceed that of the former, because the Lord (Jesus Christ) was to come to this temple, and fill it with his glory. See Haggai, <reference osisRef="Hag.2.1-Hag.2.9">Hag 2:1-9</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ezra.3"/> <div eID="gen14750" type="x-p"/>

entries.202af9028a818eaeca70855873734d51167f8e5f: <div eID="gen6341" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Altar of Burnt-Offering Erected, the Feast of Tabernacles Celebrated, and the Foundations of the Temple Laid - Ezr 3:1-13</title> <div sID="gen6342" type="x-p"/> On the approach of the seventh month, the people assembled in Jerusalem to restore the altar of burnt-offering and the sacrificial worship, and to keep the feast of tabernacles (Ezr 3:1-7); and in the second month of the following year the foundations of the new temple were laid with due solemnity (Ezr 3:8-13). Comp. 1 Esdr. 5:46-62.<hi type="italic">The building of the altar, the restoration of the daily sacrifice, and the celebration of the feast of tabernacles.</hi> - <div eID="gen6342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6343" type="x-p"/> Ezr 3:1 When the seventh month was come, and the children of Israel were in the cities, the people gathered themselves together as one man to Jerusalem. The year is not stated, but <hi type="italic">the</hi> year in which they returned from Babylon is intended, as appears from Ezr 3:8, which tells us that the foundations of the temple were laid in the second month of the second year of their return. The words, ”and the children of Israel were in the cities,” are a circumstantial clause referring to Ezr 2:70, and serving to elucidate what follows. From the cities, in which each had settled in his own (Ezr 2:1), the people came to Jerusalem as one man, i.e., not entirely (Bertheau), but unanimously (ὁμοθυμαδόν, 1 Esdr. 5:46); comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.8.1">Neh 8:1</reference>; Jdg 20:1.<note placement="foot">The more precise statement of 1 Esdr. 5:46, εἰς τὸ εὐρύχωρον τοῦ πρώτου πυλῶνος τοῦ πρὸς τῇ ἀνατολῇ, according to which Bertheau insists upon correcting the text of Ezra, is an arbitrary addition on the part of the author of this apocryphal book, and derived from Neh 8:1.</note>
entries.f5a9ad3f7b334de4535862dd45a00c7e530c9ba7: Ezr 3:2 <div eID="gen6343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6344" type="x-p"/> Then the two leaders of the people, Joshua the high priest and Zerubbabel the prince (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.2.2">Jos 2:2</reference>), with their brethren, i.e., the priests and the men of Israel (the laity), arose and built the altar, to offer upon it burnt-offerings, as prescribed by the law of Moses, i.e., to restore the legal sacrifices. According to Ezr 3:6, the offering of burnt-offerings began on the first day of the seventh month; hence the altar was by this day already completed. This agrees with the statement, “When the seventh month approached” (Ezr 3:1), therefore before the first day of this month.
entries.3411387e65b61b6a59bcfcdb6678a84ac52f6513: Ezr 3:3 <div eID="gen6344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6345" type="x-p"/> They reared the altar על־מכונתו, upon its (former) place; not, upon its bases. The feminine מכונה has here a like signification with the masculine form מכון, Ezr 2:68, and מכוּנה, Zec 5:11. The Keri מכונתיו is an incorrect revision. “For fear was upon them, because of the people of those countries.” The ב prefixed to אימה is the so-called ב <hi type="italic">essentiae</hi>, expressing the being in a condition; properly, a being in fear had come or lay upon them. Comp. on ב <hi type="italic">essentiae</hi>, Ewald, §217, f, and 299, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, though in §295, <hi type="italic">f</hi>, he seeks to interpret this passage differently. The “people of those countries” are the people dwelling in the neighbourhood of the new community; comp. Ezr 9:1; Ezr 10:2. The notion is: They erected the altar and restored the worship of Jahve, for the purpose of securing the divine protection, because fear of the surrounding heathen population had fallen upon them. J. H. Mich. had already a correct notion of the verse when he wrote: <hi type="italic">ut ita periculi metus eos ad Dei opem quaerendam impulerit.</hi><note placement="foot">Bertheau, on the contrary, cannot understand the meaning of this sentence, and endeavours, by an alteration of the text after 1 Esdras, to make it signify that some of the people of the countries came with the purpose of obstructing the building of the altar, but that the Israelites were able to effect the erection because a fear of God came upon the neighbouring nations, and rendered them incapable of hostile interference.</note> <div eID="gen6345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6346" type="x-p"/> Comp. the similar case in 2Ki 17:25., when the heathen colonists settled in the deserted cities of Samaria entreated the king of Assyria to send them a priest to teach them the manner of worshipping the God of the land, that thus they might be protected from the lions which infested it. The Chethiv ויאל must be taken impersonally: “one (they) offered;” but is perhaps only an error of transcription, and should be read ויּעלוּ. On the morning and evening sacrifices, see on Exo 28:38., Num 28:3.
entries.fcfb5e9a9f80d344f735f23a8dc097571ae8aa15: Ezr 3:4 <div eID="gen6346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6347" type="x-p"/> They kept the feast of tabernacles as prescribed in the law, Lev 23:34. “The burnt-offering day by day, according to number,” means the burnt-offering day by day, according to number,” means the burnt-offerings commanded for the several days of this festival, viz., on the first day thirteen oxen, on the second twelve, etc.; comp. Num 29:13-34, where the words כּמשׁפּט בּמספּרם, Num 29:18, Num 29:21, Num 29:24, etc., occur, which are written in our present verse כּם בּמספּר, by number, i.e., counted; comp. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.28">1Ch 9:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.31">1Ch 23:31</reference>, etc.
entries.e0ba2326f45b8019d8cb704a04e5056e2f39f905: Ezr 3:5-6 <div eID="gen6347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6348" type="x-p"/> And afterward, i.e., after the feast of tabernacles, they offered the continual, i.e., the daily, burnt-offering, and (the offerings) for the new moon, and all the festivals of the Lord (the annual feasts). עלות must be inserted from the context before לחדשׁים to complete the sense. “And for every one that willingly offered a free-will offering to the Lord.” נדבה is a burnt-offering which was offered from free inclination. Such offerings might be brought on any day, but were chiefly presented at the annual festivals after the sacrifices prescribed by the law; comp. Num 29:39. - In Ezr 3:6 follows the supplementary remark, that the sacrificial worship began from the first day of the seventh month, but that the foundation of the temple of the Lord was not yet laid. This forms a transition to what follows.<note placement="foot">Bertheau, comparing Ezr 3:6 with Ezr 3:5, incorrectly interprets it as meaning: “From the first day of the seventh month the offering of thank-offerings began (comp. Ezr 3:2); then, from the fifteenth day of the second month, during the feast of tabernacles, the burnt-offerings prescribed by the law (Ezr 3:4); but the daily burnt-offerings were not recommenced till after the feast of tabernacles, etc. <hi type="italic">Hence it was not from the first day of the seventh month</hi>, but subsequently to the feast of tabernacles, that the worship of God, so far as this consisted in burnt-offerings, was fully restored.” The words of the cursive manuscript, however, do not stand in the text, but their opposite. In Ezr 3:2, not thank-offerings (זבהים or שׁלמים), but burnt-offerings (עלות), are spoken of, and indeed those prescribed in the law, among which the daily morning and evening burnt-offering, expressly named in Ezr 3:3, held the first place. With this, Ezr 3:5, “After the feast of tabernacles they offered the continual burnt-offering, and the burnt-offerings for the new moon,” etc., fully harmonizes. The offering of the continual, i.e., of the daily, burnt-offerings, besides the new moon, the feast-days, and the free-will offerings, is named again merely for the sake of completeness. The right order is, on the contrary, as follows: The altar service, with the daily morning and evening sacrifice, began on the first day of the seventh month; this daily sacrifice was regularly offered, according to the law, from then till the fifteenth day of the second month, i.e., till the beginning of the feast of tabernacles; all the offerings commanded in the law for the separate days of this feast were then offered according to the numbers prescribed; and after this festival the sacrifices ordered at the new moon and the other holy days of the year were offered, as well as the daily burnt-offerings, - none but these, neither the sacrifice on the new moon (the first day of the seventh month) nor the sin-offering on the tenth day of the same month, i.e., the day of atonement, having been offered before this feast of tabernacles.</note>
entries.5aeb32c0ccd836da84d2bb258118895b5b96a7ee: Ezr 3:7 <div eID="gen6348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6349" type="x-p"/> Preparations were also made for the rebuilding of the temple; money was given to hewers of wood and to masons, and meat and drink (i.e., corn and wine) and oil to the Sidonians and Tyrians (i.e., the Phoenicians; comp. <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.4">1Ch 22:4</reference>), to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea of Joppa (i.e., to the coast of Joppa), as was formerly done by Solomon, 1Ki 5:6., 2Ch 2:7. כּרשׁיון, according to the grant of Cyrus to them, i.e., according to the permission given them by Cyrus, sc. to rebuild the temple. For nothing is said of any special grant from Cyrus with respect to wood for building. רשׁיון is in the O.T. ἁπ. λεγ.; in Chaldee and rabbinical Hebrew, רשׁא and רשׁי mean facultatem habere; and רשׁוּ power, permission.
entries.51870322796f4bfe7fc8dcbfed8004e5bd078467: Ezr 3:8-13 <hi type="italic">The foundation of the temple laid.</hi> - Ezr 3:8 In the second year of their coming to the house of God at Jerusalem, i.e., after their arrival at Jerusalem on their return from Babylon, in the second month, began Zerubbabel and Joshua to appoint the Levites from twenty years old and upwards to the oversight of the work (the building) of the house of the Lord. That is to say, the work of building was taken in hand. Whether this second year of the return coincides with the second year of the rule of Cyrus, so that the foundations of the temple were laid, as <hi type="italic">Theophil. Antioch. ad Autolic</hi>. lib. 3, according to Berosus, relates, in the second year of Cyrus, cannot be determined. For nothing more is said in this book than that Cyrus, in the first year of his reign, issued the decree concerning the return of the Jews from Babylon, whereupon those named in the list, Ezra 2, set out and returned, without any further notice as to whether this also took place in the first year of Cyrus, or whether the many necessary preparations delayed the departure of the first band till the following year. The former view is certainly a possible though not a very probable one, since it is obvious from Ezr 2:1 that they arrived at Jerusalem and betook themselves to their cities as early as the seventh month of the year. Now the period between the beginning of the year and the seventh month, i.e., at most six months, seems too short for the publication of the edict, the departure, and the arrival at Jerusalem, even supposing that the first year of Cyrus entirely coincided with a year of the Jewish calendar. The second view, however, would not make the difference between the year of the rule of Cyrus and the year of the return to Jerusalem a great one, since it would scarcely amount to half a year. ויּעמידוּ...החלּוּ, they began and appointed, etc., they began to appoint, i.e., they began the work of building the temple by appointing. Those enumerated are-1. Zerubbabel and Joshua, the two rulers: 2. The remnant of their brethren = their other brethren, viz., <hi type="italic">a</hi>, the priests and Levites as brethren of Joshua; <hi type="italic">b</hi>, all who had come out of captivity, i.e., the men of Israel, as brethren of Zerubbabel. These together formed the community who appointed the Levites to preside over, i.e., to conduct the building of the temple. For the expression, comp. 1 Chron 23:4-24.

                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Now in the second year of their coming unto the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, began Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the remnant of their brethren the priests and the Levites, and all they that were come out of the captivity unto Jerusalem, and appointed the Le<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vites from twenty years old and upward, to set for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward the work of the house of the LORD.</ns0:p>

                     </ns0:note> to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether, to set forward the workmen <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By their presence and favour to encourage them to a chearful and vigorous prosecution of the work.</ns0:note> in the house of God: the sons of Henadad, <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> their sons and their brethren the Levites.<ns0:note place="bottom">Not the High-Priest so called, but a Levite, of whom see <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2. 40.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, they set the Priests in their apparel with trumpets, and the Levites the sons of Asaph, with cymbals to praise the LORD, after <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap> hands.</ns0:note> the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chr. 6. 3<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. & 16. 7. & 25. 1.</ns0:note> ordinance of David <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>By,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>According to the hands of David, i. e.</ns0:hi> in such manner, and with such Psalms, or Songs, and Instruments as God had appointed by the Hands or Ministry of <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> king of Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And they <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ex. 15<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 2 Chr. 7. 3.</ns0:note> sang together by course, in praising and giving thanks unto the LORD; because <ns0:hi>he is</ns0:hi> good, for his mercy <ns0:hi>endureth</ns0:hi> for ever towards Israel: And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the LORD, because the foundation of the house of the LORD was laid.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 But many of the priests and Levites, and chief of the fathers, <ns0:hi>who were</ns0:hi> ancient men, that had seen the first house <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Which divers of them might very well do; because it was de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stroyed not quite Sixty years ago, as is manifest from 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 25. 2 <ns0:hi>Chr.</ns0:hi> 36. & <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 40. 1.</ns0:note>, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Partly because of the poor and small preparations made for this in comparison of what was made for the other Temple: partly because this Temple was divested and destitute of those things which were the principal Glory of the former Temple, to wit, the Ark<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and the Urim and Thummim, & <ns0:hi>c.</ns0:hi> partly because these foundation-stones were far inferiour to the former, both for quantity and price, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 7. 9, 10. and partly because these foundations were of a far narrower compass than the former: for although the foundations of this House of the Lord, strictly so called, were at least of equal largeness with those of the former, by comparing 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 6. 2. & <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> 6. 1, 2, 3. yet the Foundations of the whole building belonging to the first Temple, and adjoining to it, or in the courts of it, were far larger than these.</ns0:note>; and many shouted for joy:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy, from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off.</ns0:p>
